In this course we will use JupyterLite to work with Python for data analysis. 

JupyterLite is a browser-based version of Python that allows us to get up and running quickly without having to install anything on our machines. The exercises you've done in the "Introduktion til Livets Molekyler" course use the same technology under the hood, but we will now use a more full-fledged version as we work towards doing more complex tasks with Python.

## JupyterLite Introduction

JupyterLite can be accessed at this webpage: [https://au-mbg.github.io/jupyterlite-playground/lab/index.html](https://au-mbg.github.io/jupyterlite-playground/lab/index.html)

When you first access the page, you should see something like what is shown in @fig-jupyterlite-frontpage

![The JupyterLite Homepage](figures/jupyterlite/startup_page.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-jupyterlite-frontpage}

JupyterLite is a JupyterLab distribution that runs in the browser. This means you can run 
Python programs and notebooks in JupyterLite without having to install anything. 

## Working with notebooks in JupyterLite

On the home page of JupyterLite, also called the *launcher*, you can click the button that 
says `Python (Pyodide)` to create a new notebook. You will then arrive at a page like the one shown in @fig-new-notebook.

![New notebook on JupyterLite](figures/jupyterlite/new_notebook.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-new-notebook}

This notebook is a document that can contain both code and text, with the two types separated into different cells, see @fig-cell-types. The Python you worked with in IMOL is very similar to one of these code cells.

![Notebook with a Markdown cell and a Code cell](figures/jupyterlite/example_cells.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-cell-types}

To see the output produced by code in a notebook, we need to *run* or *execute* its code cells. There are several ways to control cell execution, see @fig-run-options and the list below:

- `▶`: Runs the currently selected cell. You can also use the keyboard shortcut {{< kbd mac=Shift-Enter win=Shift-Enter >}}.
- `▶▶`: Restarts the notebook and runs all cells from top to bottom.
- `⏹`: Stops execution. This is useful when code keeps running without finishing or when you notice a mistake and do not want to wait for execution to finish.
- `↻`: Restarts the notebook without running the cells again.
- `Run`: Opens a menu with additional options for running cells.

![Options for running Code cells](figures/jupyterlite/run_options.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-run-options}

::: {.callout-note title="Run cells in order"}
When you open an exercise, start at the top of the notebook and run the cells in order. The first setup cell may take a little longer to run because it prepares the course software. If you restart the notebook, run the cells from the top again before continuing your work.
:::

## Opening course notebooks

The exercises in this course are provided as notebooks that can be opened
directly in JupyterLite. On the course website, open the exercise you want to
work on and click `Open in JupyterLite` under **Other Formats**, see @fig-opening-notebook

![Options for opening or download course notebooks](figures/jupyterlite/open_course_notebook.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-opening-notebook}

JupyterLite will open and import a copy of the exercise notebook. If the
notebook does not open automatically, locate it in the JupyterLite file browser
and double-click it.

Alternatively, click `Notebook` to download the notebook to your computer. You can then upload it to JupyterLite as described below.

## Notebooks as files

The notebooks we work with in JupyterLite are a type of file, namely an IPython notebook (`.ipynb`). Throughout the course we will work with several notebooks and it is important to 
keep track of them. 

::: {.callout-note title="Finding and organizing files on your computer" collapse=true}
This course assumes that you know how to create folders, locate downloaded
files, move and rename files, and recognize common filename extensions such as
`.ipynb`, `.csv`, and `.xlsx`.

If you are unfamiliar with working with files and folders, consult the relevant
guides below.

### macOS

- [Use the Finder on Mac](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/use-the-finder-mchlp2605/mac)
- [Organize your files in Finder](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/organize-your-files-in-the-finder-mchle9f0a1b2/mac)
- [Show filename extensions on Mac](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/show-or-hide-filename-extensions-mchlp2304/mac)

### Windows

- [Use File Explorer in Windows](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/experience/fileexplorer/file-explorer-in-windows)
- [Find your files and apps in Windows](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/experience/storage-filemanagement/find-your-files-and-apps-in-windows)
- [Common filename extensions in Windows](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/experience/storage-filemanagement/common-file-name-extensions-in-windows)

In particular, we recommend enabling the display of filename extensions. This
makes it easier to distinguish notebooks, datasets, spreadsheets, and other
types of files.
:::

You should therefore create a folder (also called a directory) on your computer in a location that you can find, perhaps in your Documents folder or in a cloud storage folder such as Dropbox, iCloud, or OneDrive. This folder could be called `fysisk_biokemi` or another name that clearly communicates its purpose. 

Once you've finished working on a notebook in JupyterLite, you should export a backup to this folder. To download the notebook to your computer, select `File > Save and Export Notebook As > Notebook (ipynb)`, as shown in @fig-save-menu.

![Menu to save a notebook to the local machine](figures/jupyterlite/save_notebook.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-save-menu}

Once you've downloaded the notebook, you should move it to the `fysisk_biokemi` directory on your computer. For example, the folder might look @fig-directory-example.

![File browser on a Mac (Finder) showing a notebook in an appropriately named directory](figures/jupyterlite/directory.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-directory-example}

### Opening a saved notebook

To continue working on a notebook that is stored on your computer, upload the `.ipynb` file to JupyterLite. Click the `⬆` button in the JupyterLite file browser and select the notebook using your computer's file browser. Once the notebook appears in the JupyterLite file browser, double-click it to open it. This is shown in @fig-upload.

![Upload a file from your computer to JupyterLite](figures/jupyterlite/upload_data.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-upload}

### Persistent storage in JupyterLite 

As you use JupyterLite, you will notice that it also saves your work. However, this is done in your browser's local storage. You should **NOT** rely on this as a mechanism to store your notebook long term, as it may be reset by, for example, clearing your browser history or cookies. It will also not persist if you use another browser or another machine. 

## Data files 

Many of the exercises we will work on in the course are about analyzing data and often this data will come in the form of files, such as `.csv` or `.xlsx`. 

You should also store these data files on your machine in the same folder (or a subfolder) as you store the notebooks. The screenshot below illustrates one way of managing this.

![File browser on a Mac (Finder) showing `fysisk_biokemi`-folder with a subfolder for data containing several data files.](figures/jupyterlite/data_directory.png){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="90%" #fig-directory}

::: {.callout-warning}
Reproducing results, including data analysis, is essential in science. It is therefore important to develop good data-management practices that allow you to return to data you have worked with previously.
::: 

You will need to upload these files to JupyterLite to work with them. Use the same `⬆` button described above for uploading a saved notebook, then select the data file using your computer's file browser.

JupyterLite has its own file system in your browser. Uploading a file creates a separate copy in this file system; it does not create a live connection to the original file on your computer. If you change the original file, you will need to upload it again for those changes to become available in JupyterLite.

It is generally easiest to keep the notebook and its data files in the same folder in JupyterLite. A file in the same folder as the notebook can be referred to by its filename, for example `experiment.xlsx`. If you organize your data in a subfolder called `data`, the corresponding relative path is `data/experiment.xlsx`.

## Working with file paths.

When you want a program to read file it needs to know where the file is this is called a "file path" (en fil sti in danish). There is no wiggle-room with these file paths, they need to be exactly correct, computers are not smart enough to know that if you asked for `dataa/abc.csv` but only `data/abc.csv` exists you probably meant that.

The file system on a computer can be represented by a tree-structure, similar to a family tree. For example, the files in @fig-directory can be represented by a tree like so

```default
fysisk_biokemi
├── data
│  ├── averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx
│  ├── trypt-absor-fluor-emission.xlsx
│  └── trypt-absor-fluor-extinction.xlsx
└── jupyterlite_intro.ipynb
```

We see that `fysisk_biokemi` is a directory, that directory contains another directory `data` and a file `jupyterlite_intro.ipynb`, the `data` folder contains three files.

When working in a notebook, we specify paths *relative* to the folder containing the notebook. You can think of the notebook as the program that is reading the file. The examples below show how the path changes when the notebook is placed in different folders.

::: {.callout-note title="The notebook is inside the `fysisk_biokemi` folder" collapse="false"}
Consider the same tree with the notebook inside the `fysisk_biokemi` folder:

```default
fysisk_biokemi
├── data
│  ├── averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx
│  ├── trypt-absor-fluor-emission.xlsx
│  └── trypt-absor-fluor-extinction.xlsx
└── jupyterlite_intro.ipynb  ← notebook running from here
```

The relative path to one of the data files would then be `data/averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx`. Starting from the folder containing the notebook, we first enter the `data` folder and then find the file `averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The notebook is outside the `fysisk_biokemi` folder" collapse="true"}
If instead the notebook were located outside the `fysisk_biokemi` folder, the tree would look like this:

```default
.
├── jupyterlite_intro.ipynb  ← notebook running from here
└── fysisk_biokemi
   └── data
      ├── averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx
      ├── trypt-absor-fluor-emission.xlsx
      └── trypt-absor-fluor-extinction.xlsx
```

The relative path to the same data file would then be `fysisk_biokemi/data/averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx`. Starting from the notebook, we first enter the `fysisk_biokemi` folder, then the `data` folder, and finally find the file.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The notebook is in another folder inside `fysisk_biokemi`" collapse="true"}
Finally, the notebook could be located in a separate folder inside `fysisk_biokemi`, as illustrated by this tree:

```default
fysisk_biokemi
├── data
│  ├── averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx
│  ├── trypt-absor-fluor-emission.xlsx
│  └── trypt-absor-fluor-extinction.xlsx
└── program
   └── jupyterlite_intro.ipynb  ← notebook running from here
```

In this case, the relative path to the data file is `../data/averag-prope-amino-acids.xlsx`. Here, `../` means “go up one folder.” Starting from the `program` folder, we first go up to `fysisk_biokemi`, then enter the `data` folder and find the file.
:::

Throughout the course we will be using the [`pandas`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/index.html) specifically we will be using the functions

- `pd.read_csv`: To read `.csv` files
- `pd.read_excel`: To read `.xlsx` files.

The syntax for `pd.read_csv` is

```python
df = pd.read_csv('path/to/file.csv')
```

And equivalent for `pd.read_excel`.


### Try it yourself

The exercises below start with a file in the same folder as the notebook and gradually introduce more complex paths.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - file-path-same-folder
#|   - file-path-child-folder
#|   - file-path-nested-folder
#|   - file-path-sibling-folder
import pandas as _pandas
import posixpath

# Expected calls and feedback used by the shared checker.
EXPECTED_CALLS = {
    "file-path-same-folder": ("read_csv", "experiment.csv"),
    "file-path-child-folder": ("read_excel", "data/protein_samples.xlsx"),
    "file-path-nested-folder": ("read_csv", "data/processed/fluorescence.csv"),
    "file-path-sibling-folder": ("read_excel", "../data/enzyme_activity.xlsx"),
}

PATH_HINTS = {
    "file-path-same-folder": "The file is in the same folder as the notebook, so no folder name is needed.",
    "file-path-child-folder": "Starting from the notebook, enter the <code>data</code> folder.",
    "file-path-nested-folder": "Starting from the notebook, enter <code>data</code> and then <code>processed</code>.",
    "file-path-sibling-folder": "Go up one folder with <code>../</code>, then enter the <code>data</code> folder.",
}

# Each valid reader/path combination returns a small fictional dataset.
MOCK_DATA = {
    ("read_csv", "experiment.csv"): {
        "sample": ["A", "B", "C"],
        "pH": [2.0, 7.0, 10.0],
        "absorbance": [0.18, 0.73, 0.41],
    },
    ("read_excel", "data/protein_samples.xlsx"): {
        "sample": ["lysate", "wash", "eluate"],
        "protein concentration (mg/mL)": [8.4, 0.6, 3.2],
        "purity (%)": [42, 18, 91],
    },
    ("read_csv", "data/processed/fluorescence.csv"): {
        "wavelength (nm)": [320, 340, 360],
        "fluorescence (a.u.)": [14.2, 48.7, 22.5],
    },
    ("read_excel", "../data/enzyme_activity.xlsx"): {
        "substrate (mM)": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0],
        "rate (µmol/min)": [0.82, 1.31, 1.68],
    },
}


class MockPandas:
    """Small stand-in for the two pandas readers used in these exercises."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.attempted_calls = []

    def _read(self, reader, path):
        self.attempted_calls.append((reader, path))

        if not isinstance(path, str):
            raise TypeError("The file path must be text in quotation marks.")

        key = (reader, posixpath.normpath(path))
        if key not in MOCK_DATA:
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"No file was found at {path!r}.")

        return _pandas.DataFrame(MOCK_DATA[key])

    def read_csv(self, path):
        return self._read("read_csv", path)

    def read_excel(self, path):
        return self._read("read_excel", path)


pd = MockPandas()
```

```{pyodide}
#| check: true
#| exercise:
#|   - file-path-same-folder
#|   - file-path-child-folder
#|   - file-path-nested-folder
#|   - file-path-sibling-folder
import posixpath

# Quarto Live evaluates the model solution after the learner's code. If only
# that solution call is recorded, the learner's call never reached the mock.
attempted_calls = envir_result["pd"].attempted_calls
attempted_reader, attempted_path = (
    attempted_calls[0] if len(attempted_calls) > 1 else (None, None)
)
expected_reader, expected_path = envir_result["EXPECTED_CALLS"][label]
path_hint = envir_result["PATH_HINTS"][label]
expected_extension = posixpath.splitext(expected_path)[1]

reader_message = (
    "Use <code>pd.read_excel</code> for an <code>.xlsx</code> file."
    if expected_reader == "read_excel"
    else "Use <code>pd.read_csv</code> for a <code>.csv</code> file."
)

if attempted_path is None:
    if expected_reader not in user_code:
        feedback = {"correct": False, "message": reader_message}
    else:
        feedback = {
            "correct": False,
            "message": "Write the path as text by putting quotation marks around it, for example <code>\"filename.csv\"</code>.",
        }
elif not isinstance(attempted_path, str):
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": "A file path must be text. Put quotation marks around the filename.",
    }
elif attempted_reader != expected_reader:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": reader_message}
elif "\\" in attempted_path:
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": f"Use <code>/</code> rather than <code>\\</code> in paths. {path_hint}",
    }
elif posixpath.isabs(attempted_path):
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": "Use a relative path starting from the notebook. You do not need the complete path from the top of the file system.",
    }
elif posixpath.normpath(attempted_path) == expected_path:
    feedback = {
        "correct": True,
        "message": "Correct! The reader and path match the file shown in the tree.",
        "type": "success",
    }
elif posixpath.basename(posixpath.normpath(attempted_path)) == posixpath.basename(expected_path):
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": path_hint}
elif posixpath.splitext(attempted_path)[1].lower() != expected_extension:
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": f"Check the file extension in the tree. This file ends in <code>{expected_extension}</code>.",
    }
elif posixpath.basename(attempted_path) != posixpath.basename(expected_path):
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": "The filename does not match the tree. Check its spelling carefully.",
    }
else:
    feedback = {
        "correct": False,
        "message": "Compare your path with the file tree and remember that paths start from the notebook's folder.",
    }

feedback
```


### Summary and tips for working with notebooks

- Start at the top of a notebook and run its cells in order. Later cells may depend on variables or packages created by earlier cells.
- Editing a cell does not run the new code. Run the cell again after making a change.
- If you change an earlier cell, rerun the cells that depend on it. When in doubt, restart the notebook and run all cells from the top.
- Use the stop button if a cell keeps running without finishing.
- When Python reports an error, read the final line of the error message first. It usually gives the most useful description of what went wrong.
- Before loading a data file, check that it is visible in the JupyterLite file browser and that its path matches its location.
- JupyterLite saves work in the browser, but this storage is not a reliable long-term backup. Regularly export your notebook as an `.ipynb` file and store it on your computer.
